title: Continuous batching and chunked prefill
summary: Continuous batching schedules the GPU one iteration at a time so finished requests leave and new ones join. Chunked prefill splits long prompts so they stop stalling everyone else's streams.
useIf: You run an inference engine for many users with mixed prompt lengths and you see throughput gaps or ITL spikes.
avoidIf: You only call a hosted API. Engine scheduling is not yours to tune, and the lever there is separating workloads.

explain.md: **Static batching** forms a batch and runs it until the slowest request finishes. Short requests leave idle slots, and new requests wait for the next batch. **Continuous batching**, introduced by Orca, schedules per iteration: a request that finishes leaves immediately and a waiting request takes its slot. On GPT-3 175B the Orca paper reports 36.9 times the throughput of FasterTransformer at the same level of latency [[tr2]].

Continuous batching still has **head-of-line blocking**. If one iteration contains a long prefill, it runs for a long time and every decode in that batch waits, so ITL spikes for every active stream. **Chunked prefill** fixes this by splitting a long prompt into near-equal chunks and batching each chunk with decodes. Sarathi-Serve calls the result a stall-free schedule and reports 2.6 times the capacity on Mistral-7B (one A100) and up to 3.7 times on Yi-34B (two A100s) compared with vLLM under tail-latency limits [[r9]].

explain.title: One scheduler iteration with chunked prefill

steps.title: Decodes first
steps.md: Every running request gets one token slot.

steps.title: Fill the budget
steps.md: Remaining tokens go to pending prefills, split into chunks if needed.

steps.title: Run one pass
steps.md: Decodes and the prefill chunk share one forward pass.

steps.title: Retire and admit
steps.md: Finished requests free blocks and waiting requests join.

explain.md: In vLLM V1 chunked prefill is on by default whenever possible. The scheduler batches all pending decodes first, then fills the remaining `max_num_batched_tokens` budget with prefills and chunks any that do not fit. Smaller values such as 2048 give better ITL because fewer prefill tokens slow each step. Larger values give better TTFT, and the docs recommend more than 8192 for throughput on smaller models and large GPUs [[tr6]].

explain.title: Chunking is a trade, not a free fix
explain.md: A chunked prompt finishes its prefill over several iterations, so its own TTFT rises somewhat. The gain is for everyone else's streams, and for capacity under a tail-latency target [[r9]].

whereToUse: Self-hosted chat and agent serving with vLLM or a similar engine

use: p99 ITL spikes line up with long prompts arriving
You need more capacity under a tail-latency limit without adding GPUs
Traffic mixes short chat turns with long document prompts
avoid: Hosted APIs where you cannot set scheduler budgets
A single-tenant offline job where only total throughput counts and ITL does not
Tiny prompts only: with no long prefills there is no stall to remove
flips: TTFT for long prompts matters more than ITL: raise the token budget
ITL is the SLO: lower the token budget and accept slower long-prompt TTFT

pitfalls.symptom: Every user's stream pauses when one user pastes a long document
pitfalls.cause: A large prefill shares the iteration with decodes
pitfalls.fix: Enable chunked prefill and lower the per-step token budget [[tr6]]

pitfalls.symptom: Throughput is low on a large GPU running a small model
pitfalls.cause: A small token budget leaves compute idle

pitfalls.symptom: Interactive latency is poor while a nightly job runs
pitfalls.cause: Bulk and interactive traffic share batches and cache on one deployment

scenarios.title: ITL spikes when long prompts arrive
scenarios.situation: A chat service on a self-hosted engine streams at 30 ms per token. When a user submits a 20,000-token document, other users' streams freeze for about a second. The SLO is p99 ITL under 100 ms.
unknowns: What is the current per-step token budget?
scenarios.question: What do you change first?

options.name: Add GPUs and spread the load
options.tradeoff: It costs money and leaves the interference in place.

options.name: Enable chunked prefill and lower the per-step token budget
options.why: Decodes run in every iteration, so no stream waits for a whole 20,000-token prefill.
options.tradeoff: Long-prompt TTFT rises, and throughput may fall a little at a small budget.

options.name: Cap max output tokens
options.why: The freeze comes from a long prefill, not from long answers.
options.tradeoff: Right when long outputs hold slots and starve newcomers.

flips.if: Long prompts are rare and users accept the pause
Fleet is large and TTFT and ITL targets conflict

scenarios.takeaway: Stalls are a scheduling problem. Chunk the prefill so decodes keep running.

scenarios.title: Overnight bulk summarisation
scenarios.situation: A nightly job summarises 300,000 documents on a self-hosted small model on large GPUs. Nobody reads the output until morning. The job must finish in 6 hours.
constraints: Throughput and cost are the goals
unknowns: Is the 6 hour window at risk at today's volume?
Can the job run on dedicated GPUs?
scenarios.question: How do you tune scheduling?

options.name: Tune for ITL with a small token budget
options.why: ITL is irrelevant here, and a small budget leaves compute idle.
options.tradeoff: Right for interactive streaming where users feel every pause.

options.name: Keep one deployment shared with chat and turn on priority
options.tradeoff: Bulk traffic still shares batches and cache with chat, risking interactive latency.

options.name: Run on dedicated capacity with a large token budget, above 8192
options.why: Large steps keep a big GPU busy and maximise tokens per hour.
options.tradeoff: Individual request latency is poor, which is acceptable offline.

flips.if: The job must share GPUs with live chat
flips.then: Cap the bulk job's concurrency and tune for chat ITL first.
Raise concurrency or add GPUs before changing scheduling.

scenarios.takeaway: The right token budget depends on whether anyone waits for a single stream.

quiz.q: Streams for all users pause for about a second whenever one long prompt arrives. What most likely causes this?
options: A large prefill shares the iteration with the decodes
The tokenizer is slow on long inputs
quiz.explain: A long prefill occupies the whole iteration, so every decode in the batch waits. Chunked prefill removes this. KV quantization, speculation and tokenization do not create synchronous pauses across all streams.

quiz.q: A scheduler has a 2,048 token budget per iteration and 10 running decodes, each using 1 token. How many iterations does a 20,000-token prompt need if every iteration gives it the remaining budget?
quiz.explain: Decodes use 10 tokens, leaving 2,038 for the prefill chunk. 20,000 / 2,038 is 9.81, so it needs 10 iterations. A larger budget finishes sooner, which is the TTFT side of the trade.

quiz.q: Order the steps of one chunked-prefill scheduler iteration in vLLM V1.
items: Fill the remaining token budget with prefill chunks
Retire finished requests and admit waiting ones
quiz.explain: Decodes are prioritised, prefill fills what is left, the pass runs, and finished requests leave so waiting ones can join on the next iteration.

flashcards.front: What does continuous batching change versus static batching?
flashcards.back: It schedules per iteration, so finished requests leave and waiting ones join at once instead of waiting for the slowest request.

flashcards.front: What does chunked prefill fix, and what does it cost?
flashcards.back: It removes decode stalls from long prefills. The chunked prompt's own TTFT rises somewhat.

flashcards.front: How does max_num_batched_tokens trade ITL against TTFT in vLLM?
flashcards.back: Smaller values (such as 2048) give better ITL. Larger values give better TTFT and throughput.
